https://youtu.be/kyICmCRp22Y?si=ryiTB_tzoWPtZ2FY

In this video (Korean), I said:

Python is a programming language, but not a proof language. So, it's impossible to write a mathematical proof in Python, unlike Lean.

Some people replied that there may be Python libraries that support proof writing, just like Lean. Is this true?
I found Prove-It, a Python-based general-purpose interactive theorem-proving assistant. Is this a Python library that enables writing proofs in Python?
There's another Python-based proof assistant called Knuckledragger.
There's also https://github.com/philzook58/knuckledragger
Of course, it's possible to create a proof assistant in Python. However, does that mean Python is also a proof language?
No.
In other words, does it imply that you can write proofs in Python?
I feel like in order to really answer that question, you'd need to have a precise definition of what a 'proof language' is.
For instance, Rocq and Isabelle are unambiguously proof assistants, but they're written in OCaml and Standard ML/Scala, respectively. Likewise, Agda is written in Haskell.
Lean also is in some sense strongly based on C++ at the moment.
That's right. However, I haven't seen anyone who contends that you can write mathematical proofs in C++ because Lean is strongly based on it.

James E Hanson said:

I feel like in order to really answer that question, you'd need to have a precise definition of what a 'proof language' is.

To be honest, I don't think I have a good one. In my opinion, any language that humans can use to construct a proof checked by a computer program is a proof language.

In principle most languages can be turned into a proof language by using the LCF style approach with opaque theorem objects that are constructed from trustworthy functions (the axioms of your system) thats e.g. how HOL light turns ocaml into a proof language and you can do the same in haskell, python, c++ and pretty much any other language that comes to mind.

James E Hanson said:

Lean also is in some sense strongly based on C++ at the moment.

How do you mean that?

Henrik Böving said:

James E Hanson said:

Lean also is in some sense strongly based on C++ at the moment.

How do you mean that?

I'm referring to the fact that stage 0 of compiling Lean compiles entirely from C++ source and stage 1 still compiles some part of the Kernel from C++ source. My impression is that the ultimate plan is to fully bootstrap, but you aren't there yet, right?

Also I guess I was thinking about the fact that Lean compiles to C (which I know isn't the same thing as C++).

stage0 of compiling Lean has not been C++ since before I joined this Zulip (2021). stage0 basically contains the output of Lean's C code generator executed onto itself. We also have an LLVM backend (that is slightly slower than the C one so it never became the default) which we could use for this purpose as well (we just don't for the performance reason).

The kernel is indeed compiled from C++ but it's also exchangeable in principle, one could use Lean4lean, nanoda or other kernels for this in theory, it's again just a default choice. There is of course the runtime of Lean that is built in C++ but we're not getting around using C/C++, Rust or some other low level language for that purpose.
I see. Perhaps I shouldn't have said 'strongly', but fortunately I did use the hedging phrase 'in some sense'.

Henrik Böving said:

We also have an LLVM backend (that is slightly slower than the C one so it never became the default)

Why is it slower?

That's a very good question, we never figured that out :D. It's by 0.3% or something on some microbenchmarks and we spent a lot of time comparing LLVM IR and it seemed to us that while they are not an exact match between what clang produces and what our backend directly produces they should end up approximately the same.

Henrik Böving said:

There is of course the runtime of Lean that is built in C++ but we're not getting around using C/C++, Rust or some other low level language for that purpose.

Also why is this necessary?

Because the runtime involves a lot of juggling with raw pointers, platform specific implementation details and manual memory effects that are not really a part of the core identity of Lean the surface level language.

Henrik Böving said:

In principle most languages can be turned into a proof language by using the LCF style approach with opaque theorem objects that are constructed from trustworthy functions (the axioms of your system) thats e.g. how HOL light turns ocaml into a proof language and you can do the same in haskell, python, c++ and pretty much any other language that comes to mind.

Thanks for your detailed explanation. Practically speaking, do you think the term 'proof language' refers only to those that have native support for theorem objects and axioms?
'Proof language' isn't a standard term as far as I know.
Hmm, is there any alternative?

On page 107 of the Metamath Zero thesis:

¹²The ability to construct such a proof object is not specific to MM0, of course; just about any proof language has the same property. However, the linearity of the proof depends heavily on subterm sharing. For example, the proof objects generated by eval_add reuse a and the subterms of b many times.

Henrik Böving said:

e.g. how HOL light turns ocaml into a proof language and you can do the same in haskell, python, c++ and pretty much any other language that comes to mind.

Let me ask another question: how practical is it to turn Python into a proof language this way?

You'd write a class Theorem and make sure as good as possible that no object of type Theorem can be constructed outside of the module it was defined in, this is obviously not possible to enforce 100% in python but that's the same for most LCF style systems. Then you write your axioms like e.g. def modus_ponens(p1, p2) which assert that p1 and p2 are Theorem of the appropriate shape and if yes return a new Theorem with the appropriate shape and then you can do pretty much everything people have done with HOL Light.
Thanks for your answer!

I might want to call that a proof metalanguage (like the original ML, used for LCF itself).

The distinction is that a proof language would be a language that you can write proofs in directly, but a metalanguage is one that talks about, or in general manipulates proofs.
Then, in HOL Light's case, is OCaml a proof metalanguage and HOL Light a proof language?
Fun fact: the "ml" in OCaml is referring to ML.

Bulhwi Cha said:

Hmm, is there any alternative?

Well in my mind there's sort of two relevant concepts, and if we're being careful it's useful to distinguish between them.

On the one hand, there are formal proof systems, which are abstract formal grammars. This includes things like Hilbert-style deduction calculus, sequent calculus, natural deduction, and the version of Martin-Löf type theory one sees in textbooks and research papers.

On the other hand, there are computer implementations of formal proof systems and related tools. This obviously includes various proof assistant or interactive theorem provers, but also to some extent things like automatic theorem provers and SMT solvers.
I made a toy implementation of Howard-Curry in Rust at one point, but I would absolutely not call Rust a proof language.

Henrik Böving said:

then you can do pretty much everything people have done with HOL Light.

Is there any reason in principle why you couldn't go beyond what's been done with HOL Light?

Kyle Miller said:

Fun fact: the "ml" in OCaml is referring to ML.

Though somewhat confusingly Caml (the language in between them) is "Categorical Abstract Machine Language", and OCaml was originally "Objective Caml".
And then ML itself stands for Meta Language

Bulhwi Cha said:

Then, in HOL Light's case, is OCaml a proof metalanguage and HOL Light a proof language?

What do you all think? Do you think this is true?

James E Hanson said:

Well in my mind there's sort of two relevant concepts, and if we're being careful it's useful to distinguish between them.

Anyway, part of the reason why I think it's important to maintain this distinction is that the real-world implementations of these things are usually meaningfully messier than the theoretical version.

For instance, the way the 'axiom' Lean.trustCompiler works is essentially a bookkeeping hack. If you literally look at it, it's just a posited term of type True, meaning that it's supposed to denote the exact same object as True.intro and so there should be no actual consequences to assuming it. And this means that the actual implementation of Lean fails to satisfy certain basic metamathematical statements, specifically in this case the deduction theorem. In most proof systems, if you're able to prove B under the assumption of axiom A, then you can prove a statement of the form A -> B, but this doesn't work with Lean.trustCompiler. (Although I should note that the new system for native_decide does fix this.)

Another example is that it's often stated that Lean is equiconsistent with ZFC+{“there exists n inaccessible cardinals":n∈N}\mathsf{ZFC} + \{\text{“there exists }n\text{ inaccessible cardinals"} : n \in \mathbb{N}\}ZFC+{“there exists n inaccessible cardinals":n∈N}, but this is only true of an idealized version of the system. The actual formal system implemented in Lean on a software level only supports around 2242^{24}224 universe levels, so it's not possible to actually prove the consistency of ZFC+“there exists 2100 inaccessible cardinals"\mathsf{ZFC} + \text{“there exists }2^{100}\text{ inaccessible cardinals"}ZFC+“there exists 2100 inaccessible cardinals" in the version of Lean you can run on your computer.
Well, I thought my initial question was easy to answer. Turns out it isn't. :sweat_smile:

Bulhwi Cha said:

What do you all think? Do you think this is true?

This is probably a decent way to think about it one thing to keep in mind is that in a lot of proof assistants, the user isn't presented an entirely clear line between the 'metalanguage' and the 'proof language' (largely by design), even if there is a way to maintain such a distinction formally. You can see this in Lean (e.g., Lean's tactics language is Lean itself), but it's even more true in a constructive context like Agda.

Most examples of proofs written in Rocq, Isabelle, or Lean are actually metaprograms that build the required proof term. (This is as opposed to systems like Metamath and Agda, in which proofs are represented in a rawer form.) So at the end of the day it's a little unclear to me what should be considered 'the proof language' in something like Lean. Is it the user-facing tactics language, or is it the raw implementation of some corresponding formal proof system?

Bulhwi Cha said:

Then, in HOL Light's case, is OCaml a proof metalanguage and HOL Light a proof language?

I'd like to comment on metalanguages of proof languages. We could follow the LCF-style approach to use Python as a metalanguage for describing various proof languages that have different sets of axioms. Therefore, Python should be distinguished from all of these proof languages. Otherwise, we would mistakenly equate proof languages whose list of axioms differs from each other.

That's why it's awkward to say "Python has such-and-such axioms." On the other hand, I'm certain we can all agree that Lean has axioms.

James E Hanson said:

So at the end of the day it's a little unclear to me what should be considered 'the proof language' in something like Lean. Is it the user-facing tactics language, or is it the raw implementation of some corresponding formal proof system?

Perhaps the following quote might be relevant.

From https://lawrencecpaulson.github.io/2022/01/05/LCF.html:

Here by the way we must distinguish between

  1. the proof document: the high-level script, written in some tactic language, given to the proof assistant
  2. the proof object: the low-level formal construction using the rules of the logical calculus

The de Bruijn criterion ignores the tactic high-level script and simply checks that the low-level proof is correct and delivers the claimed result. It is satisfied by type theory proof assistants such as Coq, where proof objects are inherent in their actual proof calculus. Its main selling point is that the checker can be written by somebody who absolutely distrusts the supplied proof. They only need to trust their own system—and the logical calculus itself.

@Philip Zucker said at 8:18 in his video about Knuckledragger:

So again, this is not any different than—this is ordinary Python syntax. It's all embedded inside of ordinary Python. You define a goal of a thing that you want to prove.
Is Knuckledragger a proof language implemented by shallow embedding within Python as its host language?

Bulhwi Cha said:

To be honest, I don't think I have a good one. In my opinion, any language that humans can use to construct a proof checked by a computer program is a proof language.

Here's my second attempt at defining a proof language, which was inspired by Kyle Miller's comment:

A proof language is a language that a human can use to construct proofs directly, without having to implement a separate embedded language to write these proofs.

Knuckledragger is written in the lcf style. It has its proof objects as python data structure, which I currently do not check but assume correct because they are produced by a trusted small interface. Python objects can be marked as immutable and constructors hidden, but it is true that it isn’t the language that most well protects the innards of data types. However, ocaml also has unsafe coercions available should you reach for them, all systems have the ability to assert axioms, so this is a matter of degree imo.

It is difficult for a proof assistant to survive antagonistic use as some llm usage recently is reminding us. The only unsoundness I’m aware that I’ve accidentally triggered so far was due to a overlooked conceptual issue in the combination of skolemization and another feature.

I do agree that the proof document and the proof objects are different. There is a sense that the python code that when run produces a proof object is also a “proof” in the same sense lean tactics and code when run produce a proof. It contains information that eventually becomes a proof object. It is an unstructured form you basically can’t do much with except run it to make the more “real” proof object and read it. Arguably it’s a higher level proof object and really the one humans read to make sense of stuff most of the time to understand the proof. Similarly because humans use it, it is the level of “proof” that llms read and produce. Both assembly and C are code.

I do have some facilities for “shallow” reflection of a subset of python into the language (z3 smtlib) of formulas. It’s fun to think about but not so sure its a good idea.

The aspect with which knuckledragger is shallow is that it is a library, not a system. I don’t think even HOLs typically perceive themselves that way despite baring their ML. I want to do library stuff. Be installable via pip. Don’t change python syntax, be usable from jupyter, depend upon and be depended upon by other libraries.
Thanks for your explanation. Am I correct in saying that SBV v11.7 contained a Haskell implementation of Knuckledragger?

I think it still does. It has been renamed. https://hackage-content.haskell.org/package/sbv-13.6/docs/Documentation-SBV-Examples-TP-ShefferStroke.html It was more inspired by what I was doing than a compatible knuckledragger kernel.
https://hackage-content.haskell.org/package/sbv-13.6/docs/Data-SBV-TP.html

very cool. I'd like to understand more of what is going on in here. Any language you embed in is going to have it's own set of tricks to make things more ergonomic (and any language would work. I've considered using bash and file permissions just for the horror of it). More rigorous chaining of smt calls via big step smt based rules using lcf style is the basic idea.

It would be impossible to have a compatible kernel at the moment, since I'm still adding and taking away kernel functions every once in a while when they seem fun or useful. It is a discovery process of what I can count on z3 to do for me or not. In principle, I should have at least of full set of HOL rules, but I doubt I do atm. Having a system like vampire at the core instead of z3 which at least has some claims to being a semidecision procedure to some reasonable chunk of logic might enable removing some kernel rules. But z3 is really fast, feature rich, and low latency, so I dunno.
